column2: On the authority of Abū ʿAbdillāh al-Nuʿmān ibn Bashīr (may Allah be pleased with them both),

who said: I heard the Messenger of Allah ﷺ say: “The lawful is clear and the unlawful is clear, and between them are doubtful matters which many people do not know. Whoever guards against the doubtful matters has kept his religion and his honour free of blame; and whoever falls into the doubtful matters falls into the unlawful,

like the shepherd who grazes [his flock] around a sanctuary, about to fall into it. Indeed, every king has a sanctuary; indeed, the sanctuary of Allah is what He has made unlawful. Indeed, in the body there is a lump of flesh which, if it is sound, the whole body is sound, and if it is corrupt, the whole body is corrupt. Indeed, it is the heart.” Agreed upon (al-Bukhārī and Muslim).
The printed text reads جفي, evidently a misprint for حمى (“the sanctuary of Allah”).

Bayyin (“clear”): evident. Umūr (“matters”): affairs and circumstances. Mushtabihāt (“doubtful”): neither clearly lawful nor clearly unlawful. “Whoever guards against the doubtful matters”: leaves them. Here the explicit noun is used where a pronoun would do, to stress the importance of avoiding doubtful things.

Istabraʾa li-dīnihi (“has kept his religion free of blame”): has sought to keep it free of deficiency; “and his honour”: by protecting it from what he would be faulted for. Al-ḥimā (“the sanctuary”): what is forbidden to all but its owner. Yartaʿa fīhi (“graze in it”): his livestock eat from it.

Alā (“indeed”): a particle that opens a statement and indicates the certainty of what follows. Muḍghah (“a lump of flesh”): a piece of flesh; what is meant is the heart, which is called qalb because it turns about (taqallub) in matters from one state to another. Al-ḥimā: the protected place, a verbal noun used in the sense of a passive participle.
Encouragement to do what is lawful and to avoid the unlawful and the doubtful.
Only a few people know the [rulings of] doubtful matters.
Preserving the matters of the religion and upholding human decency (murūʾah).
Whoever does not guard against doubtful things in his earnings and livelihood exposes himself either to having his honour attacked or to falling into the unlawful.
Blocking every means that leads to what is unlawful and forbidden.
Encouragement to reform the heart, and that by its soundness everything in a person is sound and by its corruption everything in him is corrupt.
The intellect is in the heart: “…so that they may have hearts with which to reason” [al-Ḥajj 22:46].
Choosing good, lawful earnings shows you the soundness of the heart.

This hadith guides us to the fact that what Allah and His Messenger have made lawful and what Allah and His Messenger have made unlawful are each clear and evident. The danger for the Muslim lies only in the doubtful things that are hidden from many people. Whoever leaves the things that are neither clearly lawful nor clearly unlawful

has secured the soundness of his religion, kept far from falling into the unlawful, and protected his honour from people's talk, faulting him for committing this doubtful thing. Whoever does not avoid doubtful things exposes himself either to falling into the unlawful or to people backbiting him.

Then the Messenger ﷺ gave an example of one who commits doubtful things: a shepherd grazing his camels or sheep near land that someone else has protected; his livestock are likely to graze in this sanctuary because of its good pasture and their nearness to it.

The Prophet ﷺ also indicated that outward deeds point to the inward state, whether sound or corrupt, saying that in the body there is a lump of flesh, which is the heart; [the body] is sound when it is sound and corrupt when it is corrupt.

If a person does acts of obedience and good deeds with his limbs, that points to the soundness of his heart; and if he commits sins and wrongdoing and avoids acts of obedience, that points to the corruption of his heart. Among what has been said about reforming the heart:
The printed text reads وحزمه, evidently for وحرمه (“and made unlawful”).
The cure for your heart when it hardens is five things; / keep to them and you will win goodness and success:
an empty stomach, the Qurʾān pondered, and likewise / the humble pleading of one who weeps in the hour before dawn;
likewise your standing [in prayer] in the depth of the night, at its middle, / and sitting with people of goodness and knowledge.
Another poet:
If your soul calls you one day [to something], / and there is a way to oppose it,
then oppose its desire as much as you can, for / its desire is an enemy and opposing it a friend.
